The most sensitive measurements of time and space are made with resonant optical cavities, and these measurements are limited by coating thermal noise.
The mechanical and optical performance requirements placed on coating materials, especially for interferometric gravitational wave detectors, have proven extremely difficult to meet.
The authors generalize previous work on thermal noise in two-material coatings to an arbitrary multi-material stack.
The authors develop a means of estimating absorption in these multi-material coatings.
The baseline 20-layer SiO2-Ta2O5 coating has a transmission of 0.1% and an absorption of 0.5 ppm.
Replacing the high-index material below the top 3 coating doublets with MOA, which has a lower Young's modulus and mechanical loss, reduces the Brownian noise to 70% of the baseline.
A coating with 4 SiO2-Ta2O5 doublets and 3 SiO2-MOB doublets has less than 70% of the Brownian noise of the baseline coating and only 0.8 ppm absorption.
The high refractive index of MOB means that fewer and thinner layers are needed relative to Ta2O5 to produce the same transmission.
The authors' examples show that a high-index material with low mechanical loss, but not necessarily low optical absorption, can be used to make lower noise coatings.
The material properties of a given coating layer depend not only on its constituents, but also on the manufacturing process.
The authors' expressions are related to those of previous works, with some differences in notation and conventions.
The authors ignore several correction factors, such as the thick coating correction and finite size test-mass corrections, to keep the formalism simple.
The sensitivity of the coating reflection phase to a change in layer thickness is given by a recursive relation.
The total optical absorption for the coating is calculated by summing the absorption in each layer, weighted by the power attenuation.
The authors' key conclusion is that the search for coating materials should focus on a pallet of materials that can be used together, rather than a single material that satisfies all requirements.
